title: Can a supplied Karp–Rabin fingerprint be verified in near-linear time?
formal: Given a string $S\in\{0,\ldots,\sigma-1\}^{n}$ and a prime $q$, with $\sigma,q\le n^{O(1)}$, define $h_q(x_1\cdots x_\ell)=\sum_{t=1}^{\ell}x_t\sigma^{\ell-t}\bmod q$. Can one decide in $O(n\log n)$ time whether there exist equal-length substrings $A,B$ of $S$ such that $A\ne B$ but $h_q(A)=h_q(B)$? The modulus is part of the input and cannot be replaced. The deterministic decision problem is the precise target here; the source also permits randomized certification that never accepts a colliding modulus and rejects a collision-free one only with small probability.
context:
Rolling fingerprints turn a long substring into one machine-sized value. Prefix hashes let an algorithm obtain that value without reading the substring again. Unequal fingerprints certify unequal strings, but equal fingerprints only suggest equality. A verifier would determine whether that suggestion is reliable simultaneously for every substring length in the particular input.

For example, in the binary string 001110, the length-three substrings 001 and 110 represent the integers 1 and 6. Modulo 5 their fingerprints coincide, although the strings differ. Two occurrences of 001 would not be a collision: positions are allowed to differ, and it is the substring contents that matter.

For a fixed length there are only linearly many substrings, but repeating the check independently over all lengths creates quadratic work. The hoped-for improvement must share information between lengths. Checking only a predetermined pattern or only the substring comparisons actually made by one application supplies a weaker guarantee.

There is an important existing workaround: verify power-of-two lengths, then represent a general substring by a pair of overlapping power-of-two fingerprints. This changes the fingerprint being certified. It does not certify the single supplied polynomial residue at every length, so it does not settle this question.
why: I include this because it separates fast probabilistic equality tests from fast certification of the hash itself. Near-linear verification of a supplied modulus would make a common assumption in string data structures checkable at nearly the cost of reading the input, while clarifying which composite-fingerprint workarounds are actually necessary.
definitions: Use a word RAM with word size $\Theta(\log n)$, enlarged by a fixed constant to hold the polynomially bounded alphabet symbols and modulus. Arithmetic on a constant number of words costs $O(1)$. Substrings may overlap. The quantified lengths range from $1$ through $n$. This is certification for a fixed string and fixed modulus, not a universal collision-free hash for all strings.

progress.text: Karp and Rabin introduce randomized fingerprinting for pattern matching; a short residue supports efficient comparisons but can identify unequal strings.

Navarro surveys an $O(n\log n)$ expected-time construction of a composite collision-free substring fingerprint, formed from two verified power-of-two pieces. Its guarantee concerns the composite representation.
Farach-Colton explicitly asks for linear or $O(n\log n)$ verification of the given prime against all equal-length substring pairs, and records a straightforward quadratic-time solution.

review_note: Individually written from the cited primary sources. The importance assessment is editorial. New preprint proofs have not been independently verified.
answer_criterion: Give a deterministic O(n log n)-time verifier for every supplied string and modulus, or prove that no such verifier exists in the stated word-RAM model. Certifying a replacement composite fingerprint does not answer this question.

importance.reason: A concrete test of whether a widely used randomized string primitive can be certified at almost its construction cost; narrower than the general compressed-access barriers.
